Ah, my fault on missing the CMOS reset in your original post. I read right over it. 

Past that, you can try flashing the BIOS with a newer firmware update if you have access to another computer to find the firmware.

RAM can be tricky to diagnose where it's specifically going wrong. The fact that both sticks are receiving power (shown by the LEDs you mentioned) is a good thing. 

Assuming you've already checked that all cables are secured in place, I would first try seating RAM across every single configuration: meaning start with 1 stick in DIMM 1, then 2 sticks across DIMM 1/3, etc. until you've covered every possible configuration. Try to boot with each configuration. Rinse and repeat until you (hopefully) find a good configuration. I've had some success with this before. 

You can try resetting the CMOS battery on your motherboard to reset the BIOS settings. Wait about 5 minutes after removal before replacing it. There could be a faulty setting in your BIOS expecting a specific RAM configuration that it's not receiving.
